subtitle: Plan a Task 1 report and a Task 2 essay in four steps, write them for real against the clock, then download a clean copy for your teacher to mark.
t1Prompt: The pie charts below show the modes of transport used by commuters in the town of Fenwick in 2005 and 2024. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant. Write at least 150 words.
t1Step1H: Rewrite the introduction sentence in your own words — don't copy the prompt.
t1Step2H: What are the two or three biggest changes between the years? No numbers yet.
t1Step3H: Which categories will you group together first? Note the key figures.
t1Step4H: Group the rest, and note at least one direct comparison.
t1WriteH: Aim for 150 to 180 words. Use your planning notes above, but write in full sentences.
t2Prompt: Some people believe that unpaid work experience benefits young people by giving them valuable skills, while others see it as a form of exploitation. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
typeInstr: Click the type you think this is. You'll see straight away whether you're right.
t2Step1H: Rewrite the topic sentence in your own words.
t2Step2H: One sentence stating your overall view — this becomes your thesis.
t2Step3H: One idea, explained, with a specific example.
t2Step4H: The opposing view or your second point, with its own example.
t2WriteH: Aim for at least 250 words. Introduction, two body paragraphs, conclusion.
tkMeta: FOR THE MARKING TEACHER — NOT AUTO-GRADED, BY DESIGN
tkIntro: Each studio produces a plain-text file with the student's plan and their finished writing, ready to open and mark by hand. Nothing here is auto-scored — this page is a quick reference for marking, not a marking engine.
critTAP: Does the answer do what the prompt actually asked? For Task 1: is there a clear overview, and are the right features selected? For Task 2: is the exact question answered, with ideas developed and supported rather than just listed?
critCCP: Is the writing organised into clear paragraphs, each built around one main idea? Do linking words connect ideas naturally, without feeling forced or repeated too often?
critLRP: Is the vocabulary varied and precise for the topic? Look for genuine paraphrasing of the prompt rather than its exact words repeated back.
critGRP: Is there a mix of simple and complex sentences? How frequent are the grammar errors, and do any of them get in the way of understanding?
essayExpl: "Discuss both views and give your own opinion" is the signal phrase for a Discussion essay — present both sides fairly, and make your own position clear in the introduction and again in the conclusion.
t1Check0: I paraphrased the prompt without copying it
t1Check1: My overview has no numbers in it
t1Check2: I supported each body paragraph with specific figures
t1Check3: I made at least one direct comparison
t2Check0: I answered the exact question that was asked
t2Check1: I have one clear topic sentence per body paragraph
t2Check2: Each idea is supported with a specific example
t2Check3: My conclusion doesn't introduce any new ideas
tkCheck1: Clear paragraphs, each doing one job (usually four)?
tkCheck2: Task 1: overview present with no data. Task 2: position clear from the introduction?
tkCheck3: Task 1: at least one comparison. Task 2: one example per idea?
tkCheck4: Topic sentences open each body paragraph?
tkCheck5: Range of linking words, not just "and" / "but"?
tkCheck6: Recurring grammar mistakes worth flagging for next lesson?
